name: Note to Self
tagline: Impressive is easy. Exact is what you're after.
epigraph: A careful 1887 book on whisky hardly mentions casks. The vanilla here is for them.
glassware: tall highball glass (about 300 ml), chilled in the freezer, 1-inch ice cubes added one at a time

sources: Studio fact card `_studio/fact-cards/alfred-barnard.md`. *The Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails*: BARNARD, ALFRED (pdf 211–212, signed Dave Broom), PAXARETE (pdf 1483), MATURATION (pdf 1265), BOTANICAL (pdf 321), HIGHBALL (pdf 1005), Irish whiskey (pdf 1079, 2153), colour (pdf 2206). *The Cocktail Codex*, Highball (pp. 199, 208, 211, 214). *The Flavor Matrix*, vanilla (pdf 256; whiskey among its best pairings). open_items: The gap the story turns on, his book's "virtual absence of any mention of casks", is Oxford's (Dave Broom's) description; Barnard's own book hasn't been read (library gap: *The Whisky Distilleries of the United Kingdom*, 1887; repr. 1987 Mainstream, later Birlinn). The reading says "hardly mentions", never "never mentions" or "missed".

Why the casks are missing is unknown (card C1): Oxford reads it as casks being thought unimportant then, while its PAXARETE entry says producers "greatly prized" ex-sherry casks. So the reading says "We don't know why" and never pairs the gap with paxarete.
The book's year is 1887 (text and four entries); Oxford's bibliography cites an 1889 edition (C2). The scope is Britain and Ireland, not "Britain" (C3).

The bourbon-cask note in the recipe follows Hester's H5 wording ("ideally one whose label says"); no named bottle. The colour in the image brief (pale straw) is the image's choice from Oxford's range for barrel-aged spirit, not a claim about every bottle.
